restatement.intent: Describe each operation once as a data record (arguments with types, units, defaults, limits, redirects, result fields, flags, docs, implementation) and make checking, help, refusals and tests all read that one record, so they cannot disagree.
restatement.problem: When several consumers each keep their own idea of what an operation accepts and returns, they drift apart and the caller gets silent wrong behaviour instead of a precise refusal.
restatement.solution: Register one OpRecord per (receiver kind, name), keyed and validated at registration for structure and consistency. A binder turns raw calls into bound, checked arguments plus warnings (or a failure); a diagnoser converts failures into refusals using the same record's valid names, nearest match and redirects; a describer renders a short context line and full help; a walker test calls every record with sample arguments and compares results to declared fields. Anything that cannot be a record lives in one visible exceptions list, and any other list of operations is a bug.

quiz.answer: It binds: the call is accepted with a warning carrying spec.usualHint, and the warning travels with the bound call into the result the caller reads — not just a log. Hard limits refuse, usual ranges only warn, and both are checked in the declared unit before conversion at evaluation.
quiz.where: Solution; Collaborations steps 2 and 4; Implementation note 2

quiz.answer: The walker test: registration is supposed to refuse a callable record with no samples, and the walk (TestSchemaProperty in goja-cv) checks that a row-returning result's keys are exactly the declared fields, with only optional ones missing.
quiz.where: Structure (Walker); Collaborations 6; Sketch ('the walker test'); Implementation note 5

quiz.answer: Because a redirect added to one table is invisible to the others: help, the unknown-method refusal and the look/box redirect can each teach a different correction for the same near-miss, which is exactly the drift the registry exists to remove.
The binder (validates calls, produces warnings) and the describer (agent context line, full help); equally the diagnoser and the walker test.

transfer.why: Three independent consumers (LLM tool description, app controls, hub-side validation) plus frequent third-party additions is the pattern's stated trigger; the registry is the only thing that keeps the voice assistant, the app and the hub from disagreeing about what set_temperature accepts.

participants.Operation record: set_temperature, dim_lights, lock_door, run_scene — on a device kind, with args, result/state fields, flags and run (or expand, e.g. run_scene = graph of other actions)
participants.Argument spec: target: number, unit C, min/max from the device class, usual [16,24] with hint, valueDocs for enum modes; level: 0–100 %; scene: enumeration with value docs
participants.Flags: class (climate/lighting/security), confirm for lock_door and run_scene, internal for hub housekeeping actions; the host sets confirm, a plug-in cannot lower it
participants.Registry: keyed by device kind + action name; validates plug-in records at hub start-up (defaults in limits, redirects exist, samples present, (kind,name) unique)
participants.Binder: shared by the voice bridge and the app: type/limit checks in declared units, usual-range warnings, cross-argument hooks (mode vs target)
participants.Describer: one context line per callable record for the LLM tool schema; argument specs drive one widget per argument in the app; full help on request
participants.Diagnoser: turns 'switch_lights'/'brightness' near-misses into refusals naming valid actions and the fix call, using the same records
participants.Walker: per-plug-in CI test: bind samples, run in a simulator, compare result/state fields to declared fields

transfer.sketch:
value OpRecord: name, on: DeviceKind, args: [ArgSpec], validate?(args) → ok | Failure,
                returns: StateKind, fields(boundArgs) → [FieldSpec],
                flags: {class, confirm?, internal?}, redirects?, samples, doc, run | expand

registry.register(rec) → ok | refuse(E_BAD_RECORD, …)
  -- plug-in record validated like a built-in; default outside min/max, redirect to a missing
  -- action, or no samples fails hub start-up
  -- plug-in record may raise confirm but never lower it (lock_door, run_scene)

bind(deviceKind, action, raw) → BoundCall(rec, args, warnings) | Failure    -- one path for voice and app
explain(failure)    → Refusal(valid actions, nearest name, fix)            -- same record
toolSchema(rec)     → context line for the language model (internal: false only)
controlSpecs(rec)   → app widget per ArgSpec (type, unit, min/max, options, valueDocs)
-- walker, run in plug-in CI: bind(samples) → run(simulator) → keys(v) vs fields(call.args)
key_notes: Note 1 (validate structure and consistency) matters most: third-party records are the only unaudited input, so default-inside-limits, existing redirect targets and samples must fail registration at hub start-up, not reach a voice command later.

Note 2 (hard limits vs usual ranges, in the declared unit): a thermostat in °C and a dimmer in % must be checked before any conversion; out-of-usual targets bind with a spoken/app warning rather than being refused.
Flags / `confirm`: the host, not the plug-in, decides which actions need confirmation; otherwise a bad plug-in silently unlocks lock_door for a non-interactive voice run.
Note 6 (pluggable argument types): device-specific types (temperature with unit, colour, scene reference) must be addable by a plug-in without touching the binder core.
Note 7 (one record per receiver kind and name): light.dim and scene.dim are separate records with their own args; do not overload by argument type inside a kind.

Note 4 (redirects in the records): voice near-misses ('brightness', 'switch_lights') are the normal case, so option- and action-level redirects belong in the records so help and refusals teach the same correction.
Note 9 (exception list): device discovery and state-polling endpoints cannot be records; keep them in one list with a test that every name the assistant can reach is either registered or listed.
transfer.risk: Letting each side keep a shadow copy: plug-ins shipping their own help/validation strings and the mobile app hard-coding an action list, so the registry becomes a third opinion rather than the only one — usually combined with trusting the plug-in's confirm/limit flags.

transfer.why: The chapter's Applicability excludes exactly this case: when the platform already gives you the records (a typed RPC schema generating clients, docs and validation), use that schema as the registry instead of building a parallel one. A hand-built Go registry would be a second source of truth for the same methods and would drift from the .proto in the first week.

participants.Operation record: already the .proto method plus its annotations — not a new Go record
participants.Argument spec: already the .proto fields with constraint annotations
participants.Describer / Binder: already generated clients, generated docs and generated server-side validation

key_notes: Applicability, third exclusion ('the platform already gives you the records'): the proposal is the anti-case; the correct move is to extend the .proto, not to add a Go table.

Note 1 still applies, relocated: rules the proto cannot express (cross-argument hooks) should be validated server-side at start-up next to the generated code, so there is one authority rather than two.

Note 8 (defaults are part of identity, renames need redirects) applies to the .proto: add fields with defaults, deprecate rather than rename, and keep the validation annotation in sync with the generated docs.
Note 5 style applies cheaply: a walker that reflects over the generated descriptors and calls every method with sample requests is worth having, but it reads the proto, not a second registry.
transfer.risk: Building the Go registry 'just for help text', then re-implementing validation there because it is convenient, leaving two disagreeing validators and a documented default that the server does not apply.

review_notes.note: The sketch says registration checks 'samples present for every callable record' and the walker comment says 'registration guarantees samples exist', but note 5 says goja-cv keeps the walk's sample arguments in the test file and only suggests moving them into the record. A reader cannot tell whether a missing sample fails registration or is merely untested.
review_notes.suggestion: Pick one: either samples are a required record field validated at registration (and drop the goja-cv aside), or they are walker data and the sketch comment should say so.

review_notes.note: One note carries five separate claims: help rendering in the walk, per-receiver-kind calls, TestSchemaProperty, where samples live, and what a walk does not prove. The important limitation ('coverage, not correctness') is buried at the end.
review_notes.suggestion: Split into a note on what the walker asserts and a short note on keeping the walk's data out of the test file (or in the record).

review_notes.note: Cross-argument hooks are called out as the escape hatch for rules that do not fit a table, but the chapter never says what a hook receives, how it names the offending argument, or how the diagnoser turns a hook failure into a refusal that points at a fix. The sketch's HOOK case passes only code/args/hint, losing `where` and `fix`.
review_notes.suggestion: Show one hook example (e.g. a box that must fit the image) and state that hook failures must return the same refusal shape: kind, offending arg names, and a fix.

review_notes.note: The chapter says the describer renders two lengths and that goja-cv's full reference is eight times the short form, but says nothing about how the short form is chosen from sixty records: all of them? filtered by `internal`/class? grouped? That selection is the part a reader with a large catalogue will get wrong.
review_notes.suggestion: Add a short paragraph or implementation note on what goes into the standing context line and how operations are selected or grouped when they do not all fit.

review_notes.note: The list of structural checks omits duplicate positional slots: two specs may declare the same `position`, which makes positional binding order-dependent and silently ambiguous.
review_notes.suggestion: Add 'positions unique and contiguous' to the structural checks alongside unique argument names.

review_notes.note: Motivation uses a query engine and its 'no function matches the given argument types' error as a motivating case, while note 7 says a query engine must change the lookup to return candidate sets — an escape from the pattern's central invariant, tucked into an implementation note and left out of the sketch.
review_notes.suggestion: Move the overload discussion fully into Variations (or a dedicated subsection) and say explicitly that overloaded catalogues pay an extra cost in binding and refusal quality.

review_notes.note: The note explains cache keys, renames and redirects, but not the harder case: a saved script calls an operation whose argument was removed or whose meaning changed. Only renames get a migration story.
review_notes.suggestion: State the policy for removed arguments and changed units (refuse with a fix? keep an accepting alias?) and note that saved scripts make this a compatibility question, not just a documentation one.

review_notes.note: The section carries a lot of goja-cv-specific scaffolding ('designed after a comparison of nine prototypes', 'two prototypes did not scale radii', the Editor lab) before reaching the general problem, and the same goja-cv numbers reappear in the implementation notes.
review_notes.suggestion: Compress the prototype history to one sentence and keep the four failure modes, since those (not the prototype count) are what makes the problem concrete.

review_notes.note: The '★★ (close to invariant…)' line appears with no explanation of what the stars mean or what a reader should do differently for a two-star pattern; the Consequences do not connect to it.
review_notes.suggestion: Drop it to the overview or add one clause saying what a low rating implies (e.g. the value is in the details of validation and refusal quality, not the shape).

ratings.comment: Structure, forces and the applicability exclusions make it genuinely reusable, but the samples/walker contradiction and the under-specified hook and context-line selection are the parts a reader would trip on when applying it.
